derivation `a = ... = b`: only that chain, not every step the run made. Each line names the
rule and whether the step is read backwards; a chain through a value that was later rewritten
away names it too. When two chains are equally short both are printed, in the order the
rewrites were made.

- Failure: error value `NoAttribution` when the run was made without `explain: true`; error value `InvalidArgument` for a value of another function; error value `NoChain` when no rewrite connects the two values.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `r->explain<a, b>`
- Why it is not compiled: a run and two of its values come from the caller

#### `explain_all`

```camel
explain_all: (r: Run<F>) => Proof!
```

Every rewrite of the run `r`, in the order it made them, each naming the rule, the round, the
graph and the nodes that matched, were produced and were erased. This is the full record
`explain` narrows to one chain.

- Failure: error value `NoAttribution` when the run was made without `explain: true`; error value `InvalidArgument` for a value of another function.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `explain_all(r)`
- Why it is not compiled: a run comes from the caller

#### `why_not`

```camel
why_not: <rule: Rule, v: Node> (r: Run<F>) => string!
```

Why the rule `rule` did not fire at the value `v` of the run `r`: the first place the left side
fails to match, the value the pattern wanted there and the value the program has, a missing
permission, or the rule's condition being false with the values it read. A rule that did fire
at `v` is reported as such.

- Failure: error value `NoAttribution` when the run was made without `explain: true`; error value `InvalidArgument` for a value of another function.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `r->why_not<target, v>`
- Why it is not compiled: a run, a rule and a value come from the caller

### Reading a rule

#### `rule_name`

```camel
rule_name: (r: Rule) => string
```

The name of the rule `r`.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `rule_name(r)` gives `'int_add_zero'`
- Why it is not compiled: a rule comes from the library

#### `rule_two_way`

```camel
rule_two_way: (r: Rule) => bool
```

Whether the rule `r` may also be applied from right to left.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `rule_two_way(r)` gives `false`
- Why it is not compiled: a rule comes from the library

#### `rule_needs`

```camel
rule_needs: (r: Rule) => int
```

How many rewrites the rule `r` needs before it may fire.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `rule_needs(r)` gives `0`
- Why it is not compiled: a rule comes from the library

#### `rule_consts`

```camel
rule_consts: (r: Rule) => int
```

How many constants the rule `r` adds to the function.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `rule_consts(r)` gives `0`
- Why it is not compiled: a rule comes from the library

<a id="tiles"></a>

## `tiles`: programs on a CUDA device

Programs on a CUDA device. Where a computation runs is asked for in the source with the tag
`#gpu`, written on a function, a block or a namespace block (design principles 13.4), and the
card is chosen when the program runs, with `--devices`. The pass `tiles::compile` reads
the tags, outlines the regions the device can run, compiles them and runs the program: an
operator the device cannot run inside a `#gpu` scope is a compile error that names the operator
and the scope, never a quiet fall back to the host. An array on the device is an ordinary array
value whose data block lives there; the host reading it (printing, writing a file, turning it
into a host number) downloads it, and the reports of a run list every such transfer.

What a program does by hand is small: ask whether a device is there (`available`, `device`), move
a value (`upload`, `download`), and look at what would run (`source`, `inspect`, `benchmark`,
`regions`). The device and the driver are one resource, `driver`, so every call here keeps its
written order against the others and is never folded, merged or dropped. The functions to look
at are the `with` argument and the data is the example input, as for `map`:
`inputs->inspect<fn>`.

The functions that compute their type from an argument (`upload`, `download`, `source`,
`inspect`, `benchmark`, `regions`, and `run_preferred_resident`, the entry `tiles::compile` and
the tests use) are in `stdlib/signatures/tiles.cml`.

#### `upload`

```camel
upload: (value: f32[..]) => Device<f32[..]> uses driver
```

Uploads every leaf of the value -- an array, or a scalar of the element type it is written
with, alone or inside a tuple or a struct -- and gives the same tree with each leaf wrapped in
`Device<...>`. A leaf of any other type is refused when the call is compiled.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `host->upload` gives `a Device<f32[..]>`
- Why it is not compiled: the value comes from the caller

#### `download`

```camel
download: (value: Device<f32[..]>) => f32[..] uses driver
```

Downloads every device leaf of the value and gives the host value it came from. A tree with a
leaf that is not a device value is refused when the call is compiled.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `resident->download` gives `the array resident holds`
- Why it is not compiled: the value comes from the caller

#### `run_preferred_resident`

```camel
run_preferred_resident: <fn: (a: f32, b: f32) => f32> (inputs: (f32, f32)) => Device<f32> uses driver
```

Runs the function through the device path the pipeline prepared for it -- the device when a
program can be made for it, the host otherwise -- and gives the resident form of its result.
This is the operator `tiles::compile` inserts for an outlined region and the tests use; a
program asks for the device with `#gpu`, not with this.

- Example: `(f32(2.0), f32(3.0))->run_preferred_resident<(a: f32, b: f32): f32 => a + b>` gives `a Device<f32>`

#### `source`

```camel
source: <fn: (a: f32, b: f32) => f32> (inputs: (f32, f32)) => string uses driver
```

The CUDA source the function compiles to, without running it.

- Example: `(f32(2.0), f32(3.0))->source<(a: f32, b: f32): f32 => a + b>`

#### `inspect`

```camel
inspect: <fn: (a: f32, b: f32) => f32> (inputs: (f32, f32)) => string uses driver
```

A report on the function's device plan, without running it: the kernel, its launch shape and
the values it would keep on the device.

- Example: `(f32(2.0), f32(3.0))->inspect<(a: f32, b: f32): f32 => a + b>`

#### `benchmark`

```camel
benchmark: <fn: (a: f32, b: f32) => f32> (inputs: (f32, f32)) => string uses driver
```

Times the function on the device, and on the host for comparison, and gives the report as JSON
text.

- Example: `(f32(2.0), f32(3.0))->benchmark<(a: f32, b: f32): f32 => a + b>`

#### `regions`

```camel
regions: <fn: (a: f32, b: f32) => f32> () => string uses driver
```

The regions the compiler would take for the whole program, as text: which nodes would run on
the device and why the others would not.

- Example: `regions<(a: f32, b: f32): f32 => a + b>()`

#### `available`

```camel
available: () => bool uses driver
```

Whether this machine can run a program on a CUDA device: false when the driver, the toolkit or
a visible device is missing. A capability question only -- a device the run names with
`--devices` and that is not there is a fault at start-up, never `false`.

- Example: `available()`

#### `device`

```camel
device: () => string! uses driver
```

A description of the CUDA device the run selects: its ordinal, name, compute capability and
memory.

- Failure: error value `DeviceUnavailable` when this build or this machine has no CUDA device.
- Example: `device() !! 'no device'`

<a id="pyplot"></a>

## `pyplot`: draw an array

Plots: draw an array of numbers with matplotlib, and fall back to an SVG file when matplotlib
is not installed. The operator writes an image file and is never folded or dropped by a pass.

The declarations of the operator of the C++ module `modules/pyplot` (design principles 6.4).
This file is the one source of its fixed signature; the C++ side
keeps the kernel, the executor, the operator traits and the purity.

`plot` is one operator with one URI, over four element types and two arities: an array of
`i32`, `int`, `f32` or `float`, with or without the name of the output file. A declaration
cannot write "an array of one of these four" as one rule, and a declaration generic over `T`
would accept a `string[]` that the kernel refuses, so the four types are written out for each
arity: eight declarations of the one operator. A declaration cannot write the optional
parameter `filename?: string` either, which is why the two arities are separate.

#### `plot`

```camel
plot: (data: i32[]) => void
plot: (data: int[]) => void
plot: (data: f32[]) => void
plot: (data: float[]) => void
plot: (data: i32[], filename: string) => void
plot: (data: int[], filename: string) => void
plot: (data: f32[], filename: string) => void
plot: (data: float[], filename: string) => void
```

Draws the values of `data` and writes the image to `filename` (`plot.png` when it is omitted).
`data` may be an `i32`, `int`, `f32` or `float` array; an empty array is drawn as an empty
plot. matplotlib is used when it is importable, and an SVG file is written otherwise.

- With effects: writes an image file.
- Example: `plot([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], "myplot.png")`

<a id="python"></a>

## `python`: the embedded interpreter

Camel calling Python: run code in an embedded interpreter, import modules, read attributes and
call what they hold. A `PyObject` is a handle into the interpreter, not a value of the program;
it is released when nothing refers to it any more, so there is nothing to dispose of by hand.
Values cross the boundary by copy: `to_py` makes the Python object of a Camel value, in the
Python form of its type, and `from_py` reads a Python object as a value of the type the call
names.

The Python form of a type:
  - `bool`, the integer types, the float types and `string` are the Python scalars of the same
    name, by value; `Bytes` is `bytes`;
  - a tuple is a `tuple`, a struct a `dict` of its fields by name, an array a `list`, and a map
    with string keys a `dict`, each of them by its parts;
  - `PyObject` itself passes through as it is.
What converts is a table, never whatever Python would accept: `bool` takes a bool only (not `5`),
the integers take an int that fits and not a bool or a float, the floats take a float or an int
and refuse a number the type cannot hold, `string` takes a str and not bytes.

Python code can do anything, including write files and print, and the interpreter holds state
between calls. So no function here names a resource of its own: each is a use of everything, in
the written order, never folded, merged or dropped, and it runs when its result is needed or it
is in a `sync` block. Whatever Python itself refuses -- an exception, a missing module, a missing
attribute -- is an error value of kind `PythonError` whose message is the exception, its text and
its traceback, never a fault of Camel's.

The interpreter is started the first time a function here runs.
The other direction, Python calling Camel, is the package `camel` (`pip install camel-lang`).

#### `exec`

```camel
exec: (code: string) => void!
```

Runs Python statements in the interpreter. Definitions and assignments stay visible to later
calls, as in a Python session.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when the code raises.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `exec('x = 1')`
- Why it is not compiled: runs Python code when it runs, and the example only has the `void!` result to show

#### `eval`

```camel
eval: (expression: string) => PyObject!
```

Evaluates a Python expression and gives its value.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when the expression raises.
- Example: `eval('1 + 2 * 3')->to_string !! ''` gives `'7'`

#### `run_file`

```camel
run_file: (path: string) => void!
```

Runs the Python script at the path.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when the file cannot be read or the script raises.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `'scripts/hello.py'->run_file`
- Why it is not compiled: runs Python code when it runs, and the example only has the `void!` result to show

#### `import_module`

```camel
import_module: (name: string) => PyObject!
```

Imports a Python module (`'math'`, `'numpy'`, `'matplotlib.pyplot'`) and gives it. Importing runs
the body of the module and records it in `sys.modules`.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when the import raises.
- Example: `import_module('math')->attr<'pi'>->to_string !! ''` gives `'3.141592653589793'`

#### `attr`

```camel
attr: <name: string> (obj: PyObject) => PyObject!
```

The attribute of a Python object; a dotted name walks the chain. Asking may run a property or
a descriptor, so it can raise.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when the attribute does not exist or its getter raises.
- Example: `import_module('math')->attr<'pi'>`

#### `call`

```camel
call: <fn: PyObject, kwargs: Map<string, PyObject>? = null> (args: PyObject[]) => PyObject!
```

Calls a Python callable with the arguments the array holds, in order, and the keyword arguments
the callable was bound with. `call<fn>` is a function from an array of arguments to a result, so
it can be bound once and applied again.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when the call raises.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `[2.0->to_py !! eval('0')]->call<sqrt>`
- Why it is not compiled: the callable is a Python object from `attr`, which the page does not show

#### `to_string`

```camel
to_string: (obj: PyObject) => string!
```

The `str()` of a Python object, as text.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when `__str__` raises.
- Example: `eval('[1, 2]')->to_string !! ''` gives `'[1, 2]'`

#### `to_py`

```camel
to_py: (x: T) => PyObject! when has_python_form::<T>()
```

The Python object that stands for a Camel value, in the Python form of its type.

- Failure: error value `PythonError` when the interpreter cannot make the object.
- Example: `2.0->to_py->to_string !! ''` gives `'2.0'`

#### `from_py`

```camel
from_py: (obj: PyObject) => T! when has_python_form::<T>()
```

The Camel value of type T that a Python object holds. T is written at the call
(`from_py::<int>(obj)`) or taken from the type of the position the call stands in.

- Failure: error value `PythonTypeError` when the object does not have the type T (the message gives the path of the mismatch and what was found there); error value `PythonError` when reading it raises.
- Example: `eval('1 + 2')->from_py::<int> !! 0` gives `3`

<a id="nn"></a>

## `nn`: neural-network primitives

Neural-network primitives: 2-D convolution and its gradients, max and average pooling with
their gradients, batch normalization, embedding, the fused softmax cross-entropy loss, the
optimizers, and the checkpoint writer for a parameter tree. The operators work on the core
array type; nothing here needs PyTorch or a GPU.

### Convolution

#### `conv2d`

```camel
conv2d: (input: f32[..], kernel: f32[..], bias: f32[..], stride?: int, padding?: int) => f32[..]
```

2-D convolution: `input` is `[N, C, H, W]` f32, `kernel` is `[O, C, KH, KW]` f32 and `bias` is
`[O]` f32. `stride` defaults to 1 and `padding` to 0; the result is `[N, O, OH, OW]` f32 with
`OH = (H + 2*padding - KH) / stride + 1` and `OW` likewise. An input or kernel that is not
rank 4, or a window that does not fit, is refused when the call is compiled.

- Pure.
- Example: `conv2d(input, kernel, bias, 1, 0)` gives `[N, O, OH, OW]`

#### `conv2d_input_grad`

```camel
conv2d_input_grad: (input: f32[..], kernel: f32[..], dy: f32[..], stride?: int, padding?: int) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of `conv2d` with respect to its input, given the upstream gradient `dy` shaped
like the convolution's result; the result is shaped like `input`.

- Pure.
- Example: `conv2d_input_grad(input, kernel, dy, 1, 0)` gives `like x`

#### `conv2d_kernel_grad`

```camel
conv2d_kernel_grad: (input: f32[..], kernel: f32[..], dy: f32[..], stride?: int, padding?: int) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of `conv2d` with respect to its kernel, given `dy` shaped like the convolution's
result; the result is shaped like `kernel`.

- Pure.
- Example: `conv2d_kernel_grad(input, kernel, dy, 1, 0)` gives `like w`

#### `conv2d_bias_grad`

```camel
conv2d_bias_grad: (bias: f32[..], dy: f32[..]) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of `conv2d` with respect to its bias: the sum of `dy` over the batch and the
spatial axes, shaped like `bias`.

- Pure.
- Example: `conv2d_bias_grad(bias, dy)` gives `like b`

### Pooling

#### `max_pool2d`

```camel
max_pool2d: (input: f32[..], kernel: int, stride?: int, padding?: int) => f32[..]
```

Max pooling over a square window of `kernel` on `input` `[N, C, H, W]` f32. `stride` defaults
to `kernel`, `padding` to 0, and the result is `[N, C, OH, OW]`. A window that lies entirely in
the padding contributes -inf (the identity of the maximum).

- Pure.
- Example: `max_pool2d(input, 2)` gives `[N, C, H/2, W/2]`

#### `avg_pool2d`

```camel
avg_pool2d: (input: f32[..], kernel: int, stride?: int, padding?: int) => f32[..]
```

Average pooling over a square window of `kernel`: the window's elements plus +0 for those in
the padding are summed in an f64 accumulator and divided by `kernel*kernel`. `stride` defaults
to `kernel`, `padding` to 0, and the result is `[N, C, OH, OW]`.

- Pure.
- Example: `avg_pool2d(input, 2)` gives `[N, C, H/2, W/2]`

#### `max_pool2d_grad`

```camel
max_pool2d_grad: (input: f32[..], dy: f32[..], kernel: int, stride?: int, padding?: int) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of `max_pool2d` with respect to its input, given `dy` shaped like the pooling
result; the result is shaped like `input`.

- Pure.
- Example: `max_pool2d_grad(input, dy, 2)` gives `like x`

#### `avg_pool2d_grad`

```camel
avg_pool2d_grad: (input: f32[..], dy: f32[..], kernel: int, stride?: int, padding?: int) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of `avg_pool2d` with respect to its input, given `dy` shaped like the pooling
result; the result is shaped like `input`.

- Pure.
- Example: `avg_pool2d_grad(input, dy, 2)` gives `like x`

### Batch normalization

#### `batch_norm`

```camel
batch_norm: (input: f32[..], mean: f32[..], var: f32[..], gamma: f32[..], beta: f32[..], eps?: number) => f32[..]
```

Inference-mode batch normalization: `(input - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) * gamma + beta`, with
`eps` defaulting to 1e-5. Every tensor is f32 and the result is shaped like `input`.

- Pure.
- Example: `batch_norm(input, running_mean, running_var, gamma, beta)`

#### `batch_norm_train`

```camel
batch_norm_train: (input: f32[..], gamma: f32[..], beta: f32[..], running_mean: f32[..], running_var: f32[..], momentum?: number, eps?: number) => (f32[..], f32[..], f32[..])
```

Training-mode batch normalization: normalizes `input` with the batch statistics, and answers
`(y, new_running_mean, new_running_var)`, where `y` is shaped like `input` and the running
statistics are shaped like `running_mean`/`running_var`. `momentum` defaults to 0.1 and `eps`
to 1e-5.

- Pure.
- Example: `let (y, mean, variance) = batch_norm_train(input, gamma, beta, running_mean, running_var)`

#### `batch_norm_train_grad`

```camel
batch_norm_train_grad: (input: f32[..], gamma: f32[..], dy: f32[..], eps?: number) => (f32[..], f32[..], f32[..])
```

The gradients of training-mode batch normalization: `(dx, dgamma, dbeta)`, shaped like
`input`, `gamma` and `beta`. Only `y` carries gradient; the running-statistics blend is not
differentiated, so the operator takes `dy` (the gradient of `y`) and `eps`.

- Pure.
- Example: `let (dx, dgamma, dbeta) = batch_norm_train_grad(input, gamma, dy)`

### Embedding

#### `embedding`

```camel
embedding: (table: f32[..], indices: f32[..]) => f32[..]
```

Gathers rows of the rank-2 int-or-float table `[rows, dim]` by the rank-1 integer indices; the
result is `[indices.length, dim]`. An index outside `[0, rows)` is a fault.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when an index is outside the table.
- Example: `embedding(table, indices)` gives `[2, dim]`

#### `embedding_table_grad`

```camel
embedding_table_grad: (table: f32[..], indices: f32[..], dy: f32[..]) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of `embedding` with respect to its table: unvisited rows stay zero, and the
result is shaped like `table`.

- Pure.
- Example: `embedding_table_grad(table, indices, dy)` gives `like table`

### Loss

#### `softmax_cross_entropy`

```camel
softmax_cross_entropy: (logits: f32[..], target: f32[..]) => float
softmax_cross_entropy: (logits: f32[..], target: f32[..] | number[]) => float
```

The mean softmax cross-entropy of rank-2 `logits` `[batch, classes]` against a same-shaped
target distribution. When the target is an integer array or a rank-1 integer tensor it is
read as one class label per row (the URI `nn:softmax_cross_entropy_labels`), and the value is
the same as the one-hot form's.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when a label is outside `[0, classes)`.
- Example: `softmax_cross_entropy(logits, target)` gives `a float`

#### `softmax_cross_entropy_grad`

```camel
softmax_cross_entropy_grad: (logits: f32[..], target: f32[..], dy: number) => f32[..]
softmax_cross_entropy_grad: (logits: f32[..], target: f32[..] | number[], dy: number) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of `softmax_cross_entropy` with respect to `logits`, scaled by `dy`; the result is
shaped like `logits`. The label form (the URI `nn:softmax_cross_entropy_labels_grad`) takes
integer class labels instead of a target distribution and answers the same shape.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when a label is outside `[0, classes)`.
- Example: `softmax_cross_entropy_grad(logits, target, 1.0)` gives `like logits`

### Optimizers

#### `sgd`

```camel
sgd: (params: P, grads: P, lr: float) => P
```

One step of stochastic gradient descent on a parameter tree: `params - grads * lr`, with the
result shaped like `params`. `grads` must be the gradient of `params` and `lr` is a number.

- Pure.
- Example: `let next = sgd({ w: 1.0 }, { w: 0.1 }, 0.1)`

#### `adam_state`

```camel
adam_state: (params: P) => OptimizerState
```

The initial `OptimizerState` of a parameter tree: zero first and second moments, and step 0.
The state's moment trees are shaped like `params`.

- Pure.
- Example: `let state = adam_state({ w: 1.0 })`

#### `adam`

```camel
adam: (params: P, grads: P, state: OptimizerState, lr: float, beta1?: number, beta2?: number, eps?: number) => (P, OptimizerState)
```

One step of Adam on a parameter tree: answers `(new_params, new_state)`, both shaped like
`params`/`state`. `beta1` defaults to 0.9, `beta2` to 0.999 and `eps` to 1e-8.

- Pure.
- Example: `let (next, state) = adam({ w: 1.0 }, { w: 0.1 }, adam_state({ w: 1.0 }), 0.001)`

#### `save_params`

```camel
save_params: (params: P, dir: string) => void
```

Saves every tensor leaf of `params` under `dir`, as `<dir>/<path>.npy`, the path joining struct
field names and tuple indices with dots; other leaves are ignored. The directories are
created when missing.

- With effects: writes files under `dir`.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the directory cannot be created or a leaf cannot be written.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `save_params({ w: new([1.0, 2.0]), b: new([0.0]) }, 'checkpoints/step-1')`
- Why it is not compiled: the example builds its tensors with `new` from the `tensor` module, which this page does not import

<a id="optim"></a>

## `optim`: optimizers written in Camel over `tree`

The optimizers: `sgd` and `adam`, each a value, with `init` and `update` the two pure functions
a training loop calls.

    let opt = adam(cosine_decay(0.001, steps, 0.0001));
    let state = init(opt, model);
    let (model, state) = update(opt, model, gradient, state);

A schedule is a function `(step: int) => float`: `constant(rate)`, `linear_decay(peak, total,
floor)` and `cosine_decay(peak, total, floor)` build one, and the rate the update of step `n`
uses is `schedule(n)`, with `n` numbered from one. `params` is a tree of nested structs and
tuples whose leaves are numbers and tensors, and `grads` is the gradient of that tree, which
`with_grad` or `grad` gives; a tree that merely has the same type as the parameters is refused.

Every number is computed in double and rounded once, when it is stored. The arithmetic follows the
element type the leaf's own type writes: a tensor leaf of `adam` is widened to f64 and updated
there, and stored back at the element type the leaf has, so a trajectory written here is the
trajectory `modules/tensor/kernels/update.h` defines, bit for bit.

#### `constant`

```camel
constant: (rate: float) => (step: int) => float
```

The same rate at every step.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `constant(0.1)(3)` gives `0.1`

#### `linear_decay`

```camel
linear_decay: (peak: float, total: int, floor: float) => (step: int) => float
```

A rate that falls from `peak` to `floor` in a straight line: `peak * (1 - step / total)` below
step `total`, and exactly `floor` from there on. `total` is at least one.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `linear_decay(0.1, 4, 0.0)(2)` gives `0.05`

#### `cosine_decay`

```camel
cosine_decay: (peak: float, total: int, floor: float) => (step: int) => float
```

A rate that falls from `peak` to `floor` along a cosine: `floor + (peak - floor) *
(1 + cos(pi * step / total)) / 2` below step `total`, and exactly `floor` from there on.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `cosine_decay(0.1, 4, 0.0)(1)` gives `0.08535533905932738`

#### `sgd`

```camel
sgd: (schedule: (step: int) => float) => Sgd
```

Plain stochastic gradient descent: `p - rate * g` at every leaf, the rate of the step taken.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `sgd(constant(0.1))`

#### `adam`

```camel
adam: (schedule: (step: int) => float, beta1: float = 0.9, beta2: float = 0.999, eps: float = 0.00000001, decay: float = 0.0) => Adam
```

Adam. The constants default to the ones the reference kernel's callers use: beta1 0.9, beta2
0.999, eps 1e-8, and a decoupled weight decay of zero.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `adam(constant(0.001))`
- Example: `adam(constant(0.001), beta1: 0.5, eps: 0.0001)`

#### `adamw`

```camel
adamw: (schedule: (step: int) => float, beta1: float = 0.9, beta2: float = 0.999, eps: float = 0.00000001, decay: float = 0.01) => Adam
```

`adam` with a decoupled weight decay, 0.01 by default: the parameter is first moved by
`rate * decay` of itself, and the adaptive update then works on the moved parameter; the moments
see the gradient alone, which is what makes the decay decoupled.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `adamw(constant(0.001))`
- Example: `adamw(constant(0.001), decay: 0.1)`

#### `init`

```camel
init: (opt: Sgd, params: P) => SgdState
```

The state `sgd` starts from: no moments to carry, only the step count.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `init(sgd(constant(0.1)), { w: 1.0 })` gives `{ step: 0 }`

#### `init`

```camel
init: (opt: Adam, params: P) => AdamState<P>
```

The state `adam` starts from: the two moment trees at zero, shaped like the parameters, and the
step count.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `init(adam(constant(0.1)), { w: 1.0 })` gives `{ m: { w: 0.0 }, v: { w: 0.0 }, step: 0 }`

#### `update`

```camel
update: (opt: Sgd, params: P, grads: G, state: SgdState) => (P, SgdState)
```

One `sgd` update: `(params, state)`, with the step advanced by one and the rate taken from
`opt.schedule` at the step this update takes, numbered from one.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `update(sgd(constant(0.1)), { w: 1.0 }, { w: 0.5 }, init(sgd(constant(0.1)), { w: 1.0 }))`

#### `update`

```camel
update: (opt: Adam, params: P, grads: G, state: AdamState<P>) => (P, AdamState<P>)
```

One `adam` update: `(params, state)`, with the step advanced by one and the rate taken from
`opt.schedule` at the step this update takes, numbered from one. A `decay` other than zero moves
the parameters by the decoupled weight decay first.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `update(adam(constant(0.1)), { w: 1.0 }, { w: 0.5 }, init(adam(constant(0.1)), { w: 1.0 }))`

<a id="autodiff"></a>

## `autodiff`: gradients of functions

Automatic differentiation: function transforms that turn a function into the function of its
gradient. `grad(f)` and `with_grad(f)` take the function as an ordinary argument (it is what is
transformed, not a configuration) and give a function of the same parameters, so
`with_grad(loss)<model>(x, y)` is the loss together with the gradient of the model, and the two
steps can be written apart: `let step = with_grad(loss)`, then `step<model>(x, y)` in the loop.

What is differentiated is the first `with` parameter of `f` (the weights); every other `with`
parameter is a constant, and so is every ordinary parameter. To differentiate the data, bind it
as a `with` parameter with a lambda. A function with no `with` parameter, or whose first one has
no tangent, or a result that is not a scalar float, is refused where the call is compiled.

The gradient has the type of the parameter it is the gradient of: a struct gives a struct of
gradients, a tuple a tuple, an array of floats an array of the same element type and shape, a
float a float of its own type. An integer or a bool leaf is not a continuous quantity: its
gradient is a zero of its own type, so a parameter tree that carries a counter can be updated by
leaving the counter as it is. A string or a function leaf has no gradient and is refused with
the path of the leaf named. A value that depends on the differentiated parameter but has no way
for its gradient to flow (an array of strings read inside a loop) is refused as well, never
dropped.

`grad` and `with_grad` are the transforms of reverse mode, built on the pass mechanism: they
need `std::macro` to have expanded what they differentiate, and they leave a call whose callee is
not known when they run to a run-time refusal. `vjp` is reverse mode for a result that is not a
scalar (it gives the result and the pullback from the cotangent of the result to the gradient),
and `jvp` is forward mode (the result and its tangent along a direction); both land with the
autodiff lane, not before they work.
`stop_gradient` marks a value as a constant, and a custom derivative of a function is the tag
`#vjp(rule)` on its declaration.

#### `grad`

```camel
grad: (f: F) => Gradient<F> when is_function::<F>()
```

The gradient function of `f`: it takes the parameters of `f` and gives the gradient of `f`'s
result with respect to its first `with` parameter, in the type of that parameter.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `let loss_grad = grad(loss)`
- Why it is not compiled: `loss` must have a `with` parameter for its gradient to exist, and that takes a declaration, so the example is a fragment of a program that declares it

#### `with_grad`

```camel
with_grad: (f: F) => ValueAndGradient<F> when is_function::<F>()
```

The value and the gradient together: the function it gives returns `(result of f, gradient)`,
the pair a training step needs from one evaluation. The same compile-time refusals as `grad`.

- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `let step = with_grad(loss)`
- Why it is not compiled: `loss` must have a `with` parameter for its gradient to exist, and that takes a declaration, so the example is a fragment of a program that declares it

#### `stop_gradient`

```camel
stop_gradient: (x: T) => T pure
```

Gives its argument unchanged and cuts the gradient at this point: a value passed through
`stop_gradient` is a constant to `grad`. Any value is accepted, and the result has the
argument's own type.

- Example: `stop_gradient(3.0)` gives `3.0`

<a id="sim"></a>

## `sim`: Monte Carlo simulation

Monte Carlo simulation: two kernels that estimate a number from random samples. `pi_hits`
estimates pi from the fraction of points that fall inside the unit circle and
`asian_call_price` prices a one-year Asian call by simulating the underlying's paths. Both
take the sample count and the seed, so a seed reproduces the result exactly and the operators
are pure.

#### `pi_hits`

```camel
pi_hits: (samples: int, seed: int) => int
```

Draws `samples` points uniformly from the square [-1, 1]^2 with a generator seeded by `seed`
and returns how many fall inside the unit circle. The estimate of pi is `4 * hits / samples`;
a negative sample count is a fault.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when `samples` is negative.
- Example: `pi_hits(10000, 42)` gives `7863`

#### `asian_call_price`

```camel
asian_call_price: (paths: int, steps: int, seed: int) => float
```

Prices a one-year Asian call on a geometric random walk with `paths` simulated paths of
`steps` steps each, using the fixed parameters S0 = 100, K = 100, r = 0.05 and sigma = 0.2,
and a generator seeded by `seed`; the result is the discounted average payoff. A negative
path count or a non-positive step count is a fault.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when `paths` is negative or `steps` is not positive.
- Example: `asian_call_price(2000, 128, 42)` gives `5.894325529519635`

<a id="onnx"></a>

## `onnx`: export a program as an ONNX model

Exporting Camel programs as ONNX models: `export_model` writes the model of a function applied
to an example argument, and `supported_operators` lists the operator URIs the backend can
lower. The module is the ONNX exporter, not a runtime: loading it and asking what it can lower
needs neither the ONNX runtime nor a GPU; only a run of `export_model` writes a file.

#### `supported_operators`

```camel
supported_operators: () => string[]
```

Lists the operator URIs the ONNX backend can lower at its default opset, in the order the
lowering table reports them. A capability report only: it reads the table compiled into the
module and never touches the file system or the ONNX runtime.

- Pure.
- Example: `let uris = supported_operators()`

#### `export_model`

```camel
export_model: <out: string, dynamic_axes: int[] = [], target: string = 'onnxruntime-cpu'> (fn: F, example: E) => void! when is_function::<F>()
```

Writes the ONNX model of `fn` applied to arguments like `example` to the file `out`, at the
backend's default opset. `example` is one argument of a one-parameter `fn`, or a tuple with
one example per parameter; the function's graph is translated after the generic passes, and a
node the backend cannot lower is refused. `out`, `dynamic_axes` and `target` are `with`
parameters because they are runtime values: `dynamic_axes` names the axes of the tensor inputs
that are left unknown in the model (which is what lets one model run at several shapes), and
`target` names the runtime whose capability data decides whether a node this backend lowers is
one that runtime has (`'none'` switches the check off).

- With effects: writes a file and reads the function's graph.
- Failure: error value `ExportUnsupported` when `fn` is not a function, when the graph cannot be translated (a call that remains, an operator without an ONNX lowering, a dtype or shape the exporter cannot name), or when the target runtime rejects a node; error value `IOError` when the model cannot be written.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `export_model<out: "/tmp/model.onnx">(fn, example)`
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `export_model<out: "/tmp/model.onnx", dynamic_axes: [0]>(fn, example)`
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `export_model<out: "/tmp/model.onnx", target: "onnxruntime-cpu">(fn, example)`
- Why it is not compiled: the call needs a function value and an example of the arguments that function takes, which the description introduces (the exporter reads the function's graph, so no value a fragment can write stands for it)
